tips.title: Trace each pollutant to its source
tips.body: Carbon in the fuel → **carbon dioxide**, or **carbon monoxide** and **soot** if oxygen is short. Hydrogen in the fuel → **water vapour**. Sulfur in the fuel → **sulfur dioxide**. And **nitrogen from the air** → **oxides of nitrogen**. Four sources, six products.

tips.title: Only one pollutant comes from the air
tips.body: **Oxides of nitrogen** are the exception: the nitrogen comes from the **air**, not from the fuel, and they form only because engines get **hot enough** to make nitrogen and oxygen react. Every other pollutant here traces back to something **in the fuel**.

tips.title: Incomplete combustion gives two things
tips.body: Too little oxygen gives **carbon monoxide** and **particulates** — soot and unburned hydrocarbons. Both are signs of the same cause, so a question describing a smoky, yellow flame is telling you the oxygen supply is limited.

tips.title: Carbon monoxide is dangerous because it hides
tips.body: It is **toxic**, and it is **colourless and odourless**, so it is **not easily detected**. The second half is why it kills: you cannot tell it is there. An answer giving only *toxic* has left out what the specification emphasises.

tips.title: Two cause acid rain, one causes dimming
tips.body: **Sulfur dioxide** and **oxides of nitrogen** cause **respiratory problems and acid rain**. **Particulates** cause **global dimming** and health problems. Keeping those two groups apart is most of what this spec point asks.

why.matters:
What comes out of a chimney is decided by two things: what was in the fuel, and how much oxygen it had. That is the whole topic, and it makes the products **predictable** rather than something to memorise.

Carbon and hydrogen with plenty of air give carbon dioxide and water. Starve the air and the carbon comes out half-burned, as carbon monoxide or as soot. Any sulfur in the fuel comes out as sulfur dioxide. Three kinds of problem, from one short list of ingredients.

examples.title: The blue flame and the yellow one
examples.body:
A gas hob burns blue. A flame that is yellow and lazy is short of air, and that is not a cosmetic difference — it is the reason a gas appliance has to be serviced and a house has a carbon monoxide alarm.

With plenty of oxygen the carbon ends up as carbon dioxide. Starved of it, some ends up as **carbon monoxide**, which is toxic and — the dangerous part — **colourless and odourless**, and some as **soot**, which is the yellow glow and the black deposit. Same fuel, different air supply, entirely different products.

visual.alt: Two equations for burning the same methane: with plenty of air it gives carbon dioxide and water and a clean blue flame, and with too little air it gives carbon monoxide and water instead

examples.title: Why the fuel is sold low sulfur
examples.body:
Coal, oil and diesel contain some sulfur, and sulfur burns too. What comes out is **sulfur dioxide**, which dissolves in the water in clouds and falls as **acid rain**.

The damage is to trees, to lakes, and to any building made of limestone — acid on a carbonate, which is a reaction you have already met. Taking the sulfur out at the refinery is cheaper than the damage, which is why the pumps say low sulfur and ships are made to burn it near land.

visual.alt: A flow chart from sulfur in the fuel: it burns to sulfur dioxide, the gas dissolves in the water in clouds, the rain that falls is acidic, and it damages limestone buildings and trees

examples.title: Why a city charges you to drive an old diesel
examples.body:
Low-emission zones are not about carbon dioxide, which does the same thing wherever it is released. They are about the pollutants that do their damage **where you are standing**.

Soot particles and unburned hydrocarbons get into lungs and cause respiratory problems, and in the air they reflect sunlight back out, which is **global dimming**. Nitrogen oxides come from the nitrogen in the air itself being hot enough in the engine to react, and they cause both acid rain and breathing trouble. All three are local, and all three are avoidable.

steps.title: What is in a fuel, and what comes out
steps.body:
**The combustion of fuels is a major source of atmospheric pollutants.**

**Most fuels, including coal, contain carbon and/or hydrogen, and may also contain some sulfur.** That short sentence is the key to the whole topic: **what comes out depends on what went in**, plus how much oxygen there was.

**The gases released into the atmosphere when a fuel is burned may include carbon dioxide, water vapour, carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen. Solid particles and unburned hydrocarbons may also be released that form particulates in the atmosphere.**

**Trace each one back to its source:**

- **Carbon in the fuel**, with **plenty of oxygen** → **carbon dioxide**
- **Carbon in the fuel**, with **too little oxygen** → **carbon monoxide** and **soot (carbon particles)**
- **Hydrogen in the fuel** → **water vapour**
- **Sulfur impurities in the fuel** → **sulfur dioxide**
- **Nitrogen and oxygen from the air**, at **high temperature** → **oxides of nitrogen**

**Notice that only the last one does not come from the fuel.** Nitrogen is not a fuel impurity — it is the gas making up four-fifths of the **air**. It reacts with oxygen only because engines run **hot enough** to force the reaction. That is why oxides of nitrogen are associated with **vehicles and furnaces** rather than with any particular fuel.

**So the question *predict the products of combustion of this fuel* is answerable** from the composition of the fuel and the conditions, which is exactly what the specification asks you to do.

steps.title: Complete and incomplete combustion
steps.body:
**With plenty of oxygen, a hydrocarbon burns completely:**

$$\mathrm{CH_4 + 2O_2 \rightarrow CO_2 + 2H_2O}$$

The carbon becomes **carbon dioxide** and the hydrogen becomes **water vapour**. Nothing else is produced, and the flame is clean and blue.

**With too little oxygen the combustion is incomplete**, and the carbon is not fully oxidised. Two things then appear:

- **Carbon monoxide**, $\mathrm{CO}$ — carbon that has taken only **one** oxygen instead of two
- **Soot**, which is **carbon particles** — carbon that has taken **none** at all

**Unburned hydrocarbons** may also escape, and together with the soot these form **particulates** in the atmosphere.

$$\mathrm{2CH_4 + 3O_2 \rightarrow 2CO + 4H_2O}$$

**The flame tells you which is happening.** Complete combustion gives a **clean blue** flame; incomplete combustion gives a **yellow, smoky** flame, because glowing soot particles are what make it yellow. A question describing a smoky yellow flame is telling you the **oxygen supply is limited**.

**Incomplete combustion also releases less energy**, because the fuel has not been fully oxidised — which is why a badly adjusted burner is both dangerous and wasteful.

**Predicting products.** Given a fuel's composition and the conditions, work through the elements: **carbon** gives carbon dioxide if oxygen is plentiful, carbon monoxide and soot if it is not; **hydrogen** gives water; **sulfur** gives sulfur dioxide. Then ask whether the temperature is high enough for **oxides of nitrogen**.

steps.title: What each pollutant does
steps.body:
**Spec point 4.9.3.2 asks you to describe and explain the problems caused by increased amounts of these pollutants in the air.** They fall into three groups.

**Carbon monoxide** is a **toxic gas**. It is **colourless and odourless and so is not easily detected**.

**Both halves of that matter.** It is poisonous because it binds to the haemoglobin in red blood cells in place of oxygen, so the blood carries less oxygen. And because you cannot see or smell it, people are unaware they are breathing it — which is why faulty heaters are dangerous and why detectors exist at all. An answer giving only *it is toxic* has left out what makes it uniquely dangerous.

**Sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen cause respiratory problems in humans and cause acid rain.**

They dissolve in water droplets in clouds to form acids, which fall as **acid rain**. That damages **buildings and statues** made of limestone, harms **trees**, and makes **lakes and rivers acidic** enough to kill fish. They also irritate the lungs and worsen conditions such as asthma.

**Particulates cause global dimming and health problems for humans.**

**Global dimming** is a reduction in the sunlight reaching the Earth's surface, because the particles **reflect sunlight back into space** and **help form more cloud**. The health problems come from the particles being small enough to be **breathed deep into the lungs**.

**Keeping the groups apart is most of what this spec point asks.** Two pollutants cause **acid rain**; one causes **global dimming**; one is dangerous because it **cannot be detected**.

steps.title: Predicting the products
steps.body:
**The specification asks you to predict the products of combustion of a fuel, given appropriate information about its composition and the conditions.** That is a method, not a memory test.

**Work through the elements in the fuel, then ask about the conditions:**

1. **Carbon** → carbon dioxide if oxygen is **plentiful**; **carbon monoxide** and **soot** if it is **limited**
2. **Hydrogen** → **water vapour**
3. **Sulfur** → **sulfur dioxide**
4. Is the temperature **high**? If so, nitrogen and oxygen **from the air** give **oxides of nitrogen**

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Trace every pollutant to a source and the topic becomes a method.** **Carbon** in the fuel gives carbon dioxide, or carbon monoxide and soot when oxygen is short. **Hydrogen** gives water vapour. **Sulfur** gives sulfur dioxide. **Nitrogen from the air** gives oxides of nitrogen. Learn the four sources rather than the six products, and an unfamiliar fuel becomes a question you can answer.

**Oxides of nitrogen are the exception, and questions exploit it.** The nitrogen is **not in the fuel** — it is the gas making up four-fifths of the **air**, and it reacts with oxygen only because engines and furnaces reach a **high enough temperature**. So a completely sulfur-free, perfectly burned fuel can still produce them, and changing the fuel does not help. That is why vehicles need **catalytic converters** rather than cleaner petrol.

**Carbon monoxide and soot are the same diagnosis.** Both mean **incomplete combustion**, which means **too little oxygen**. So does a **yellow, smoky flame** — the yellow is glowing soot. One observation, several consequences: carbon monoxide is being made, particulates are being released, and **less energy** is coming out of the fuel than it should.

**Say why carbon monoxide kills.** It is **toxic** because it binds to haemoglobin in place of oxygen, so the blood carries less oxygen. But the specification stresses the second point: it is **colourless and odourless and so not easily detected**. That is what makes it uniquely dangerous, and an answer that stops at *toxic* has left out the half that explains the fatalities.

**Keep the three groups of effects apart.** **Sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen** → **respiratory problems and acid rain**. **Particulates** → **global dimming and health problems**. **Carbon monoxide** → **toxic and undetectable**. Muddling dimming into acid rain, or giving acid rain for particulates, is the commonest error in the spec point.

**And global dimming is a specific mechanism.** Particles **reflect sunlight back into space** and **help clouds form**, so **less sunlight reaches the surface**. It is not a synonym for pollution making the sky look grey.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **The combustion of fuels is a major source of atmospheric pollutants.**
- **Most fuels, including coal, contain carbon and/or hydrogen, and may also contain some sulfur.**
- **Carbon** with plenty of oxygen → **carbon dioxide**.
- **Carbon** with too little oxygen → **carbon monoxide** and **soot (carbon particles)**.
- **Hydrogen** → **water vapour**.
- **Sulfur** in the fuel → **sulfur dioxide**.
- **Nitrogen and oxygen from the air**, at **high temperature** → **oxides of nitrogen**.
- Only **oxides of nitrogen** come from the **air** rather than the fuel.
- **Solid particles and unburned hydrocarbons** form **particulates**.
- **Incomplete combustion** gives a **yellow, smoky flame** and releases **less energy**.
- **Carbon monoxide is toxic**, and **colourless and odourless so is not easily detected**.
- **Sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen cause respiratory problems in humans and cause acid rain.**
- **Particulates cause global dimming and health problems for humans.**
- **Global dimming**: particles **reflect sunlight** back into space, so **less reaches the surface**.
- To **predict the products**, work through the elements in the fuel, then ask whether the oxygen supply is limited and whether the temperature is high.

questions.prompt: A diesel engine burns a fuel containing carbon, hydrogen and a small amount of sulfur, at high temperature and with a limited air supply. Predict the pollutants produced, explain where each comes from, and describe the problems each causes.
questions.solution:
Every pollutant can be traced to an element in the fuel or to the air, so the prediction follows from the composition and the conditions.

The air supply is **limited**, so combustion of the **carbon** is **incomplete**. Rather than being fully oxidised to carbon dioxide, some carbon takes only **one** oxygen atom and becomes **carbon monoxide**, and some takes **none** and is released as **soot**, which together with any **unburned hydrocarbons** forms **particulates**. Some carbon dioxide will still be produced, but less than with a good air supply, and **less energy** is released from the fuel than it could give.

The **hydrogen** in the fuel burns to give **water vapour**, which happens whatever the oxygen supply.

The **sulfur** impurities burn to give **sulfur dioxide**. This comes from the fuel itself, so it could be reduced by using a fuel with less sulfur in it.

The engine runs at **high temperature**, which is enough to make **nitrogen and oxygen from the air** react, producing **oxides of nitrogen**. This one is worth singling out, because the nitrogen does **not come from the fuel** — it is the gas making up four-fifths of the air. That means a cleaner fuel would not prevent it, which is why vehicles are fitted with catalytic converters instead.

The problems fall into three groups. **Carbon monoxide** is **toxic**: it binds to haemoglobin in place of oxygen, so the blood carries less oxygen. It is also **colourless and odourless and so not easily detected**, and that second point is what makes it so dangerous — people do not know they are breathing it.

**Sulfur dioxide** and **oxides of nitrogen** cause **respiratory problems in humans**, irritating the lungs and worsening conditions such as asthma, and they **cause acid rain**. Dissolving in water droplets in clouds, they form acids that fall as rain, damaging limestone buildings and statues, harming trees, and acidifying lakes and rivers enough to kill fish.

**Particulates** cause **global dimming** — the particles **reflect sunlight back into space** and help form cloud, so **less sunlight reaches the Earth's surface** — and **health problems**, because they are small enough to be breathed deep into the lungs.

questions.prompt: Explain how the products of burning a fuel depend on the composition of the fuel and on the conditions, using complete and incomplete combustion as examples.
questions.solution:
**Most fuels, including coal, contain carbon and/or hydrogen, and may also contain some sulfur.** What comes out when they burn depends on **what went in** and on **how much oxygen was available**.

With **plenty of oxygen**, combustion is **complete**. The **carbon** is fully oxidised to **carbon dioxide** and the **hydrogen** becomes **water vapour**:

$$\mathrm{CH_4 + 2O_2 \rightarrow CO_2 + 2H_2O}$$

Nothing else is produced from the hydrocarbon itself, the flame is **clean and blue**, and the maximum amount of energy is released.

With **too little oxygen**, combustion is **incomplete**, and it is the **carbon** that is affected. Some of it takes only **one** oxygen atom and is released as **carbon monoxide**; some takes **none at all** and is released as **soot**, which is carbon particles. **Unburned hydrocarbons** may escape as well, and together with the soot these form **particulates** in the atmosphere. The hydrogen still becomes **water vapour**, since it is not competing for oxygen in the same way.

Incomplete combustion is visible: the flame is **yellow and smoky** rather than blue, because glowing **soot particles** are what give it the colour. It is also **wasteful**, because carbon that has not been fully oxidised still holds chemical energy, so **less energy is released** than the fuel could give. That is why a badly adjusted burner is both dangerous and inefficient.

Two further pollutants depend on things other than the carbon and hydrogen. If the fuel contains **sulfur** — as coal typically does — it burns to give **sulfur dioxide**. This depends entirely on the **fuel**, so a low-sulfur fuel produces less of it.

**Oxides of nitrogen** are the exception to the whole pattern. The nitrogen does **not come from the fuel**: it comes from the **air**, which is about four-fifths nitrogen. At the **high temperatures** reached inside engines and furnaces, that nitrogen reacts with oxygen. Because the source is the air rather than the fuel, changing to a cleaner fuel does not prevent them — only lowering the temperature or treating the exhaust does.

So predicting the products of any fuel is a matter of working through its **elements** — carbon, hydrogen, sulfur — deciding whether the **oxygen supply** is plentiful or limited, and finally asking whether the **temperature** is high enough for the air's nitrogen to react.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Most fuels, including coal, contain carbon and/or hydrogen, and may also contain some sulfur.** What comes out when they burn depends on **what went in** and on **how much oxygen was available**.

With **plenty of oxygen**, combustion is **complete**. The **carbon** is fully oxidised to **carbon dioxide** and the **hydrogen** becomes **water vapour**:

$$\mathrm{CH_4 + 2O_2 \rightarrow CO_2 + 2H_2O}$$

Nothing else is produced from the hydrocarbon itself, the flame is **clean and blue**, and the maximum amount of energy is released.

With **too little oxygen**, combustion is **incomplete**, and it is the **carbon** that is affected. Some of it takes only **one** oxygen atom and is released as **carbon monoxide**; some takes **none at all** and is released as **soot**, which is carbon particles. **Unburned hydrocarbons** may escape as well, and together with the soot these form **particulates** in the atmosphere. The hydrogen still becomes **water vapour**, since it is not competing for oxygen in the same way.

Incomplete combustion is visible: the flame is **yellow and smoky** rather than blue, because glowing **soot particles** are what give it the colour. It is also **wasteful**, because carbon that has not been fully oxidised still holds chemical energy, so **less energy is released** than the fuel could give. That is why a badly adjusted burner is both dangerous and inefficient.

Two further pollutants depend on things other than the carbon and hydrogen. If the fuel contains **sulfur** — as coal typically does — it burns to give **sulfur dioxide**. This depends entirely on the **fuel**, so a low-sulfur fuel produces less of it.

**Oxides of nitrogen** are the exception to the whole pattern. The nitrogen does **not come from the fuel**: it comes from the **air**, which is about four-fifths nitrogen. At the **high temperatures** reached inside engines and furnaces, that nitrogen reacts with oxygen. Because the source is the air rather than the fuel, changing to a cleaner fuel does not prevent them — only lowering the temperature or treating the exhaust does.

So predicting the products of any fuel is a matter of working through its **elements** — carbon, hydrogen, sulfur — deciding whether the **oxygen supply** is plentiful or limited, and finally asking whether the **temperature** is high enough for the air's nitrogen to react.

examTechnique.body:
Learn the **four sources** rather than the six products: **carbon**, **hydrogen** and **sulfur** in the fuel, and **nitrogen from the air**. Then any question about an unfamiliar fuel is answerable from its composition and the conditions.

The effects divide into three groups, and questions test whether you can keep them apart: **acid rain** (sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen), **global dimming** (particulates), and **undetectable toxicity** (carbon monoxide).
examinerErrors: Saying the fuel must contain **nitrogen** to produce oxides of nitrogen — it comes from the **air**.
Giving only *toxic* for carbon monoxide, and omitting **colourless and odourless so not easily detected**.
Attributing **acid rain** to particulates or to carbon dioxide.
Attributing **global dimming** to a gas rather than to **particulates**.
Forgetting that incomplete combustion also releases **less energy**.
Describing a yellow smoky flame without naming **incomplete combustion** as the cause.
Predicting **sulfur dioxide** from a fuel that contains no sulfur.
Giving carbon dioxide as a product of **incomplete** combustion only, or carbon monoxide as a product of complete combustion.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer treats prediction as a **method**: work through the **elements in the fuel**, decide whether **oxygen is limited**, then ask whether the **temperature** is high enough for the air's nitrogen to react. It singles out **oxides of nitrogen** as the one pollutant whose source is the **air**, and draws the consequence — a cleaner fuel cannot prevent them. It gives **both** reasons carbon monoxide is dangerous, and it keeps **acid rain**, **global dimming** and **toxicity** attached to the right pollutants. Asked to evaluate a proposed fix, it checks whether the fix addresses the **actual source**.
